Jeremiah 1.audience: Judah's first hearers would have recognized Jeremiah as unusually young for a prophetic call and would have heard the almond-branch wordplay immediately, since shaqed (almond) and shoqed (watching) sound alike only in Hebrew, not in translation.

culture.title: An almond rod
culture.text: The almond tree (shaqed) is the first to blossom; God says he will "hasten" (shoqed, ‘watch over’) his word—a Hebrew wordplay.

culture.title: A seething pot from the north
culture.text: Invaders from Mesopotamia entered Israel from the north, following the Fertile Crescent around the desert.

culture.title: Anathoth
culture.text: Anathoth was a Levitical town a few miles north of Jerusalem (Joshua 21:18). Abiathar the priest was banished there (1 Kings 2:26).

Jeremiah 2.audience: Jeremiah's early messages remind Judah of its devotion in the wilderness and accuse it of forsaking the LORD for other gods and foreign alliances.

culture.title: Broken cisterns
culture.text: Cisterns cut into rock and plastered held rainwater; cracked ones leaked. A spring of living water was far better.

culture.title: Drinking the waters of Sihor
culture.text: Sihor is the Nile and "the river" the Euphrates—Egypt and Assyria, the two powers Judah courted.

culture.title: A wild ass in heat
culture.text: A wild donkey in season runs after a mate and cannot be held back—an image of Judah chasing other gods.

Jeremiah 3.audience: Hearers who remembered the northern kingdom's fall would have felt the force of being compared unfavorably to a nation they considered already judged and gone.

culture.title: A bill of divorce
culture.text: A husband gave a divorced wife a written certificate (Deuteronomy 24:1–4). The law forbade remarrying her after she married another.

culture.title: Sitting by the road like an Arabian
culture.text: Desert raiders waited by trade routes to ambush caravans.

Jeremiah 4.audience: Jeremiah warns of a destroyer from the north and describes the land returning to chaos, "without form, and void" (Jeremiah 4:23; Genesis 1:2).

culture.title: Blowing the trumpet
culture.text: The shofar was sounded to warn of invasion and gather people into walled cities.

culture.title: Breaking up fallow ground
culture.text: Unplowed ground had to be broken up before sowing, or seed would fall among thorns.

culture.title: Painting the face
culture.text: Women outlined their eyes with dark cosmetic (kohl). Jerusalem adorning herself will not win over her attackers.

Jeremiah 5.audience: Jeremiah searches Jerusalem's streets for one honest person and finds none among the poor or the great.

culture.title: Fed horses
culture.text: "They were as fed horses in the morning"—well-fed stallions as an image of unrestrained lust.

culture.title: Bird cages
culture.text: Fowlers kept caged birds as decoys; the houses of the wicked are full of deceit like such cages.

culture.title: Rains in season
culture.text: The former and latter rain and the appointed weeks of harvest were God's provision for the land.

Jeremiah 6.audience: Jeremiah warns the people of Benjamin to flee Jerusalem and sound the alarm at Tekoa and Bethhaccerem as an army approaches (Jeremiah 6:1).

culture.title: Signal fires
culture.text: Fire signals on hilltops passed warnings from town to town. One of the Lachish letters mentions watching for signals of Lachish.

culture.title: Peace, peace
culture.text: False prophets and priests say "Peace, peace; when there is no peace"—healing the wound lightly.

culture.title: The old paths
culture.text: Travelers asked for the well-worn roads, which were safest.

Jeremiah 7.audience: Jeremiah's temple sermon is given at the gate of the LORD's house (Jeremiah 7:2); Jeremiah 26 tells how it was received at the start of Jehoiakim's reign. Jesus quoted "a den of robbers" from verse 11 (Matthew 21:13).

culture.title: The queen of heaven
culture.text: Families baked cakes for "the queen of heaven," probably the goddess Ishtar or Astarte. Children gathered wood and women kneaded dough.

culture.title: Remember Shiloh
culture.text: Shiloh, where the tabernacle once stood, was destroyed and never rebuilt as a sanctuary.

culture.title: Tophet
culture.text: In the valley of Hinnom children were burned in sacrifice at Tophet. Josiah had defiled it (2 Kings 23:10), but it was used again.

Jeremiah 8.audience: Jeremiah grieves over a people who will not repent: "Is there no balm in Gilead?" (Jeremiah 8:22).

culture.title: Bones dug up
culture.text: Invaders sometimes desecrated royal tombs and scattered the bones—the ultimate disgrace.

culture.title: Migrating birds
culture.text: The stork, turtledove, crane, and swallow pass through the land on fixed seasons each year.

culture.title: Balm of Gilead
culture.text: Gilead was known for a healing resin traded to Egypt (Genesis 37:25).

Jeremiah 9.audience: Jeremiah wishes his head were waters and his eyes a fountain of tears for the slain of his people (Jeremiah 9:1).

culture.title: Mourning women
culture.text: Professional mourning women were hired to wail at funerals and teach their daughters laments.

culture.title: Circumcised yet uncircumcised
culture.text: Egypt, Edom, Ammon, Moab, and desert tribes also practiced circumcision; Judah is circumcised in body but not in heart.

Jeremiah 10.audience: Readers fluent in both Hebrew and Aramaic would have noticed the single Aramaic verse standing out from its surroundings, a line apparently meant to be repeated even to Aramaic-speaking foreigners as a rebuke of their own gods.

culture.title: An idol like a scarecrow
culture.text: Idols "are upright as the palm tree, but speak not"—the Hebrew may compare them to a scarecrow in a cucumber field.

culture.title: Silver from Tarshish and gold from Uphaz
culture.text: Idols were plated with imported silver and gold and clothed in blue and purple.

culture.title: Signs of heaven
culture.text: Babylonians and others read eclipses and stars as omens. Israel was not to fear them.

Jeremiah 11.audience: Hearers from Jeremiah's own priestly circles would have felt the shock of the Anathoth plot especially sharply, since it meant rejection from the prophet's own professional and family community, not just from strangers.

culture.title: The iron furnace
culture.text: Egypt is called "the iron furnace"—a smelting furnace, a picture of harsh affliction (Deuteronomy 4:20).

culture.title: A lamb led to the slaughter
culture.text: Jeremiah compares himself to a tame lamb or ox, unaware of the plot.

Jeremiah 12.audience: Readers who already knew the Jordan's thick riverside jungle as home to lions would have understood God's question as a warning that present hardship was mild compared to what still lay ahead.

culture.title: The thickets of the Jordan
culture.text: "The swelling of Jordan" is the dense jungle along the river, home to lions.

culture.title: A speckled bird
culture.text: A strange-colored bird is attacked by other birds.

Jeremiah 13.audience: Jeremiah acts out a sign with a linen girdle hidden by the river Euphrates until it is spoiled (Jeremiah 13:1–7).

culture.title: A linen girdle
culture.text: A linen sash or loincloth was worn close to the body; priests wore linen. Some think "Euphrates" (Perath) here refers to Parah, a spring near Anathoth.

culture.title: Every bottle filled with wine
culture.text: Wine was stored in large pottery jars.

culture.title: The leopard's spots
culture.text: "Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?" Both Cushites and leopards were familiar to Jeremiah's hearers.

Jeremiah 14.audience: Jeremiah describes a severe drought (Jeremiah 14:1–6). The prophets of peace promise that it will not happen.

culture.title: Empty cisterns
culture.text: Servants sent to the pits (cisterns) find no water and return with empty vessels, covering their heads in shame.

culture.title: Wild asses on the heights
culture.text: Wild donkeys stand on the bare hills sniffing the wind for moisture.

Jeremiah 15.audience: God says that even Moses and Samuel could not turn him from judgment, because of what Manasseh did in Jerusalem (Jeremiah 15:1–4).

culture.title: Moses and Samuel as intercessors
culture.text: Moses and Samuel were remembered as Israel's great intercessors (Exodus 32:11–14; 1 Samuel 7:9).

culture.title: Eating God's words
culture.text: "Thy words were found, and I did eat them"—Ezekiel later eats a scroll (Ezekiel 3:1–3).

Jeremiah 16.audience: God tells Jeremiah not to marry, mourn, or feast, as a sign of the coming disaster.

culture.title: Mourning customs
culture.text: Mourners cut themselves, shaved their heads, and shared bread and "the cup of consolation." Israel's law forbade cutting (Deuteronomy 14:1).

culture.title: Fishers and hunters
culture.text: Fishermen netted fish and hunters searched rocks and holes—no one would escape.

Jeremiah 17.audience: Later generations, especially after the exile, would have read this sermon as explaining in advance why the sabbath became such a defining mark of Jewish identity and obedience.

culture.title: A pen of iron
culture.text: Judah's sin is written with an iron stylus and a diamond point—tools used to engrave stone.

culture.title: A heath in the desert
culture.text: A desert shrub in salt land contrasts with a tree planted by water (compare Psalm 1:3).

culture.title: Carrying burdens on the sabbath
culture.text: Farmers and traders carried goods into the city through the gates; on the sabbath this was forbidden (Nehemiah 13:15–19).

Jeremiah 18.audience: Jeremiah goes down to the potter's house and watches him rework a marred vessel (Jeremiah 18:1–6).

culture.title: The potter's wheel
culture.text: Potters shaped clay on a wheel turned by hand or foot. A flawed pot could be pressed back into a lump and reshaped while still wet.

culture.title: Snow of Lebanon
culture.text: The snow on the mountains of Lebanon fed cold streams that did not fail.

Jeremiah 19.audience: Those who witnessed the broken jar would have understood immediately, from everyday experience, that fired pottery could never be put back together, making the sign impossible to misread as reversible.

culture.title: A potter's earthen bottle
culture.text: A narrow-necked clay jar, once fired, could not be repaired. Breaking it pictures irreversible ruin.

culture.title: Incense on rooftops
culture.text: People burned incense on house roofs to the host of heaven.

Jeremiah 20.audience: Hearers of Jeremiah's lament afterward would have recognized a prophet willing to voice despair openly rather than present a polished, triumphant front after suffering for his message.

culture.title: The stocks
culture.text: Stocks locked a prisoner's feet, hands, or neck in a wooden frame, often in public.

culture.title: A fire shut up in the bones
culture.text: Jeremiah tries not to speak, but God's word is "as a burning fire shut up in my bones."

Jeremiah 21.audience: Zedekiah's envoys, and anyone who heard of their mission afterward, would have expected Jeremiah to repeat past deliverances like Hezekiah's, making his refusal to promise one all the more unwelcome.

culture.title: Going out to the Chaldeans
culture.text: Jeremiah tells the people that whoever surrenders will live. Besieged cities that surrendered were often spared destruction.

culture.title: Justice in the morning
culture.text: Kings were to "execute judgment in the morning"—hearing cases at the start of the day.

Jeremiah 22.audience: Judeans who had watched these kings reign in quick succession would have heard their own recent political history summarized and judged within a single chapter.

culture.title: Building with forced labor
culture.text: Jehoiakim builds a spacious palace with cedar paneling and vermilion paint, using his neighbor's labor without wages.

culture.title: The burial of an ass
culture.text: Being "buried with the burial of an ass"—dragged out and thrown beyond the gates—meant no burial at all.

culture.title: A signet ring
culture.text: A signet ring on the right hand was a king's most valued possession. Even if Coniah were that ring, God would pull him off.

Jeremiah 23.audience: Later readers facing their own disappointing leaders would have carried this chapter's hope for a righteous Branch forward as a standing promise rather than a prediction tied to one generation.

culture.title: Shepherds as rulers
culture.text: Kings in the ancient Near East were commonly called shepherds of their people.

culture.title: The burden of the LORD
culture.text: A prophet's oracle was called a "burden" (massa). Jeremiah plays on the word: the people themselves are the burden.

culture.title: A righteous Branch
culture.text: A shoot from a royal family tree was a way to speak of a king's descendant.

Jeremiah 24.audience: Exiles who assumed deportation was pure disaster, and those left behind who assumed they were the fortunate ones, would both have had their expectations reversed by this vision.

culture.title: First-ripe figs
culture.text: The first figs of early summer were prized; spoiled figs were thrown away.

Jeremiah 25.audience: Daniel's generation, reading this prophecy decades later in exile, would have used its seventy-year figure to calculate how much longer their own captivity had left (Daniel 9:2).

culture.title: Seventy years
culture.text: Daniel later read this prophecy (Daniel 9:2), and Chronicles connects the exile's end with it (2 Chronicles 36:21).

culture.title: The cup of fury
culture.text: Jeremiah is told to make the nations drink the cup of God's fury—a list running from Egypt to Elam.

culture.title: Sheshach
culture.text: Sheshach is a coded name for Babylon, made by replacing each letter with the one at the opposite end of the Hebrew alphabet.

Jeremiah 26.audience: At the start of Jehoiakim's reign, Jeremiah's temple sermon leads to a trial. Elders recall that Micah prophesied against Jerusalem in Hezekiah's day and was not killed (Jeremiah 26:18; Micah 3:12).

culture.title: A trial at the new gate
culture.text: The princes sit in the entry of the new gate of the temple to hear the case.

culture.title: Uriah extradited from Egypt
culture.text: Jehoiakim brings back the prophet Uriah from Egypt and kills him. Vassal treaties often required returning fugitives.

culture.title: Ahikam son of Shaphan
culture.text: Ahikam, of the scribal family of Shaphan, protects Jeremiah. Shaphan had served Josiah (2 Kings 22:3).
